## Presentation Outline

- Tumors of pancreatic ductal or ductal-related origin
- Pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN)
- Ductal adenocarcinoma and variants
- Tumors associated with cystic intraductal neoplasm
- Mucinous cystic neoplasm
- Serous cystic tumors
- Lymphoepithelial cyst
- Neuroendocrine tumors of the pancreas
- Tumors with acinar differentiation
- Tumors of uncertain cell lineage
- Mesenchymal and other non-epithelial tumors
- Lymphomas
- Pseudotumors of the pancreas
- Metastatic tumors
- Tumors of ampulla and periampulla

---

## Tumors of Pancreatic Ductal or Ductal-Related Origin

- Pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN)
- Ductal adenocarcinoma and variants
- Tumors associated with cystic intraductal neoplasm
- Mucinous cystic neoplasm
- Serous cystic tumors
- Lymphoepithelial cyst

---

## Pancreatic Intraepithelial Neoplasia (PanIN) — Definition

- Noninvasive lesion confined to the pancreatic ducts
- Observed only microscopically (< 0.5 cm)
- Mucin-containing duct epithelium
- Spectrum of architectural and cytologic atypia
- Designated as:
  - Low-grade (PanIN-1 and PanIN-2)
  - High-grade dysplasia (PanIN-3)
- High-grade PanIN is the key precursor of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
- Staged as carcinoma in situ

---

## PanIN — Epidemiology and Associations

- Low-grade PanIN may be associated with:
  - Age
  - Obesity
  - Diabetes mellitus (DM)
- Found in more than 50% of people older than 50 years of age
- Molecular and genomic studies indicate high-grade PanIN is the key precursor of PD adenocarcinoma

---

## PanIN — Pathologic Features

**Low-grade PanIN (PanIN-1 and PanIN-2)**
- Flat or mildly papillated, polarized mucinous epithelium
- Mild to moderate nuclear atypia

**High-grade PanIN (PanIN-3)**
- Increased architectural complexity
- Prominent epithelial papillations
- Cribriforming
- Budding micropapillae
- Loss of cellular polarity
- Marked cytologic atypia with nuclear pleomorphism
- Frequent mitoses

---

## Figure 59.1 — Pancreatic Intraepithelial Neoplasia (PanIN)

- **A:** Low-grade PanIN-1 — small, basally oriented nuclei; flat to minimally papilled mucinous epithelium
- **B:** Low-grade PanIN-2 — mildly enlarged, basally oriented nuclei; increased papillary architecture
- **C:** High-grade PanIN-3 — marked cytologic atypia, loss of nuclear polarity, increased architectural complexity

---

## PanIN — Biomarker Expression

- Biomarker expression in high-grade PanIN usually mirrors ductal adenocarcinoma
- Positive immunoreactivity to mucin 1 (MUC1)
- Abnormal expression of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA)

---

## PanIN — Clinical Significance

- Presence of high-grade PanIN is virtually indicative of invasive adenocarcinoma in the pancreas
- When PanIN-3 is identified without established invasive adenocarcinoma:
  - Re-examine specimen thoroughly
  - Exclude occult or overlooked early-stage adenocarcinoma
- High-grade PanIN at resection margin = microscopically positive margin (R1)

---

## PanIN — Molecular Biology and Genetics

- Most PanINs (high- and low-grade) harbor KRAS mutations
- Significantly increased clonality in high-grade PanINs
- High-grade PanIN shares genetic abnormalities with invasive ductal adenocarcinoma:
  - Biallelic inactivation of CDKN2A (p16)
  - Wide spectrum of clonal copy number changes
- Lacks TP53 and SMAD4 mutations (commonly seen in invasive ductal adenocarcinoma)

---

## Ductal Adenocarcinoma and Variants — Definition

- Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC):
  - Aggressive malignant epithelial neoplasm
  - Derived from pancreatic duct
  - Predominant glandular/tubular differentiation
  - With or without mucin production

**Less common variants:**
- Adenosquamous carcinoma
- Neuroendocrine carcinoma (NEC; small-cell or large-cell type)
- Colloid carcinoma
- Anaplastic undifferentiated carcinoma
- Sarcomatoid undifferentiated carcinoma
- Undifferentiated carcinoma with osteoclastic giant cells
- Medullary carcinoma
- Hepatoid carcinoma
- Signet ring cell carcinoma
- Mixed ductal and nonductal carcinoma

---

## PDAC — Epidemiology

- Most common neoplasm of the pancreas (> 90%)
- Most cases are sporadic
- About 10% have documented familial history
  - Deleterious germline mutation identified in 10%–20% of these patients
- More commonly located in the head of the pancreas (two thirds)
- Can also occur in pancreatic heterotopia of the upper GI tract (extremely rare)
- Median age at diagnosis: approximately 70 years

---

## PDAC — Clinical Features

**Most common presentation:**
- Unexplained weight loss
- Back pain
- Jaundice
- Decreased appetite
- New-onset DM

**Rare symptoms:**
- Migratory thrombophlebitis
- Acute pancreatitis (AP)

---

## PDAC — Diagnosis

- Usually diagnosed when infiltrative solid mass detected by:
  - CT scans with multiphasic dynamic contrast
  - MRI
- Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) facilitates sampling of mass or lymph node
- Serum biomarkers: CEA and CA 19-9 may be elevated

---

## PDAC — Prognosis

- Overall 5-year survival: less than 10%
- Most effective treatment: complete surgical resection + adjuvant systemic therapy
  - 5-year survival: about 12%–20%
  - Only possible in approximately 20% of patients at diagnosis
- Neoadjuvant therapy may improve surgical resectability and survival in some cases
- Untreated or metastatic disease: mean survival less than 6 months

---

## PDAC — Macroscopic Features

- Solid firm mass with irregular contour
- Mean size of resectable lesions: roughly 3.5 cm
- Tumors in distal pancreas usually larger
- Focal cystic changes may be observed distal to tumor (duct obstruction)
- Obstruction of common bile duct (CBD) and main pancreatic duct is common (head of pancreas)
- May grossly infiltrate:
  - Ampulla
  - Duodenal wall
  - Superior mesenteric vein
  - Uncinate process
  - Retroperitoneum

---

## Figure 59.2 — Macroscopic Appearance of PDAC

- Example of ductal adenocarcinoma in the head of the pancreas near the uncinate process
- Obstructs the pancreatic duct (PD)
- Impinges on common bile duct (CBD)
- Causes distal dilatation of both ducts

---

## Conventional Ductal Adenocarcinoma — Microscopic Features

- Most PDAC has gland formation
- Significant heterogeneity in histologic pattern
- Distorted glands/tubules of varying sizes and shapes
- Large glands: cribriform and papillary pattern
- Small units: incomplete gland/tubular structure or single cell-infiltrating pattern
- Intracellular and extracellular mucin common
- Desmoplastic reaction surrounding malignant epithelium is typical
- Tumor stroma may appear hypocellular with dense pink collagen
- Epithelium: columnar or cuboidal with considerable nuclear pleomorphism
- Nuclear membrane irregular with smudged appearance
- Better differentiated PDAC: well-formed glands with vesicular/foamy intracellular mucin and condensed thickened apical border

---

## Figure 59.3 — Microscopic Appearance of PDAC

- **A:** Primary PDAC with histologic and cytologic heterogeneity
- **B:** Primary PDAC with foamy intracellular mucin and thickened atypical cytoplasmic membrane
- **C:** Metastatic PDAC to lung showing paradoxical better differentiation

---

## PDAC — Metastatic Pattern and Diagnostic Challenge

- PDAC metastases to lung and omentum may present paradoxically with better differentiation
- Diagnostically challenging during workup to exclude lung or other potential primary sites
- Immunohistochemical and molecular studies can facilitate definitive diagnosis

---

## PDAC — Immunoprofile

- Typical pancreatobiliary phenotype
- Not entirely specific
- Workup usually for diagnosis of exclusion of adenocarcinoma from other primary sites
- Tumor cells:
  - Positive for CK7
  - Negative for CK20 and CDX2
  - Express MUC1, CEA, CA125, and B72.3
- DPC4 and CDKN2A gene mutations:
  - Loss of nuclear SMAD4 expression
  - Loss of p16 expression

---

## Adenosquamous Carcinoma

- Homogenous squamous cell carcinoma of pancreas is uncommon
- Varying extents of squamous differentiation can occur with conventional ductal adenocarcinoma
- Classification requires ≥ 30% squamous component
- **Pitfall:** Exclusively squamous carcinoma may be present in small biopsies or at metastatic site
  - Raises differential of primary squamous cell carcinoma from other sites (e.g., lung)

---

## Neuroendocrine Carcinoma (NEC)

- Rare; accounts for less than 1% of pancreatic neoplasms
- Includes small-cell and large-cell variants
- Clinically, pathologically, and genetically distinct from well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor (NET)
- More akin to PDAC in pathogenesis
- Commonly associated with an adenocarcinoma component
- Frequent TP53 and RB1 mutations or inactivation of RB1/P16 pathway
- Diagnosis requires:
  - Morphologic characteristics of NEC
  - Immunoreactivity for neuroendocrine markers (chromogranin and synaptophysin)

---

## NEC — Subtypes and Grading

**Small-cell subtype:**
- Nuclear hyperchromasia and molding
- Minimal cytoplasm
- Loss of Rb protein expression in most cases

**Large-cell subtype:**
- Can be challenging, particularly in small biopsies
- Morphologic features overlap with high-grade PanNET, acinar cell carcinoma, and other solid pancreatic neoplasms

**Proliferative index (Ki67):**
- Small-cell subtype: > 80%
- Large-cell subtype: > 20%

---

## Figure 59.4 — Variants of PDAC

- **A:** Adenosquamous carcinoma
- **B:** Neuroendocrine carcinoma, non-small cell type
- **C:** Undifferentiated carcinoma with osteoclastic giant cells
- **D:** Mixed ductal (upper left) and acinar carcinoma (lower right)

---

## Colloid Carcinoma

- Variant of PDAC
- Usually derived from intestinal-type intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasia (IPMN)
- **Defining feature:** At least 80% of neoplastic epithelium suspended in mucin
- Tumor cells may have focal poorly differentiated signet ring cell morphology
- Majority arranged as strips, clusters, or glands (well to moderately differentiated)
- Immunoreactive for CK20, CDX2, and MUC2
- More favorable outcomes than conventional PDAC
- 5-year survival: greater than 55%

---

## Undifferentiated Carcinoma

- Lacks recognizable cell line of differentiation
- Hypercellularity with confluent growth pattern
- Tumor cells may have partial or complete loss of immunoreactivity for cytokeratin
- Usually positive for vimentin
- **Sarcomatoid carcinoma and carcinosarcoma:**
  - Significant component of malignant spindle cells
  - With or without heterologous elements
- Tumors with rhabdoid morphology may be associated with SWI/SNF pathway abnormalities
  - Loss of nuclear expression of SMARCA2 or SMARCA4 proteins
  - Designated as SMARC-deficient malignancies

---

## Undifferentiated Carcinoma with Osteoclastic Giant Cells

- Loss of epithelial differentiation
- Composed of both neoplastic and non-neoplastic mononuclear cells
- Includes osteoclast-like multinucleated giant cells
- Giant cells immunoreactive to histiocytic markers CD68 and CD163

---

## Mixed Ductal and Nonductal Carcinoma

- Includes:
  - Ductal-NEC
  - Ductal-acinar cell carcinoma
  - Ductal-neuroendocrine-acinar carcinoma combination
- Discussed in corresponding sections of acinar cell carcinoma and NEC

---

## PDAC — Molecular Biology and Genetics

**Somatic genetic drivers:**
- Oncogenic mutations of KRAS (> 90%)
- Mutation or deletion of:
  - TP53 (75%)
  - SMAD4 (55%)
  - CDKN2A (80%)

**Other less common somatic mutations:**
- Genes involved in DNA repair and epigenetics
- PALB2, ATM, CHEK2, RAD51

---

## PDAC — Hereditary Cases

**Well-established susceptibility genes:**
- BRCA2
- ATM
- BRCA1
- PALB2
- CDKN2A
- STK11
- PRSS1
- SPINK1
- DNA mismatch repair genes

- Majority of familial aggregations of PDAC have uncertain underlying genetic abnormalities

---

## Tumors Associated with Cystic Intraductal Neoplasm — Overview

- Group of neoplasms with prominent intraductal papillary growth pattern
- Grossly visible cystic lesions in most cases (> 5 mm)
- May involve main pancreatic duct or accessory branch ducts

**Subtypes based on epithelial phenotype:**
- Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN)
- Intraductal oncocytic papillary neoplasm (IOPN)
- Intraductal tubulopapillary neoplasm (ITPN)

- Neoplastic epithelium exhibits spectrum of histologic and cytologic atypia
- Designated as low-grade or high-grade neoplasm
- Invasive carcinoma when stromal invasion is present

---

## Intraductal Neoplasms — Epidemiology and Clinical Features

- Can occur in wide range of age groups
- More common in older adults in their 50s and 60s
- Location in head of pancreas more common than distal portion
- Lesions can be multifocal
- Most common and better evaluated: IPMN

**IPMN can involve:**
1. Main pancreatic duct with prominent dilation
2. Branch ducts with isolated cystic lesion (no apparent communication with main duct)
3. Mixed main-branch duct type

**Clinical symptoms:** Nonspecific — pain, chronic pancreatitis (CP), DM, jaundice
- In absence of invasive carcinoma, serum CEA and CA19-9 may not be elevated
- Markers may be elevated only in cyst fluid from aspiration samples

---

## IPMN — Prognosis

- Without invasive carcinoma: favorable prognosis
  - Branch-duct subtype: 5-year survival > 85%
- Main-duct subtype:
  - Often associated with multifocal lesions
  - Greater risk of high-grade dysplasia and carcinoma
  - Higher risk of recurrence
- With invasive carcinoma: depends on tumor stage and subtype
  - 5-year survival ranges from 35% to 90%
- IPMN with associated colloid carcinoma: significantly better outcome than conventional PDAC
- IOPN and ITPN with invasive carcinoma also appear to have better prognoses (may not be conclusive due to rarity)

---

## IPMN — Macroscopic Features

**Main-duct IPMN:**
- May involve a portion of duct or entire duct, including ampulla
- Mucin extrusion may be visualized by upper GI endoscopy or ERCP
- Dilated duct usually filled with mucin and soft papillary projections

**Branch-duct IPMN:**
- May lack visible connection to main duct
- Usually present as multilocular cysts filled with mucin

**High-risk features:**
- Larger IPMNs (> 3 cm)
- Mural nodules or intracystic masses
- More likely to harbor high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma

---

## Figure 59.5 — Macroscopic Appearance of IPMN

- **A:** Total pancreatectomy (head left, tail right) with multifocal IPMN involving the entire main duct
- **B:** Distal pancreatectomy with mixed main-duct and branch-duct IPMN

---

## IPMN — Microscopic Features

- Intraductal proliferation of columnar epithelium
- Abundant intracellular and extracellular mucin
- Categorized as low- or high-grade dysplasia based on:
  - Histologic complexity
  - Cytologic atypia

**Subtypes:**
- Intestinal type
- Gastric type
- Pancreatobiliary type

---

## IPMN — Intestinal Type

- Commonly associated with main-duct IPMN
- Neoplastic epithelium forms villous papillary architecture
- Tall columnar intestinal-type cells
- Elongated nuclei with apical intracellular mucin
- High-grade dysplasia commonly observed
- **Immunophenotype:**
  - Positive: CK20, CDX2, MUC2
  - Negative: CK7, MUC1

---

## IPMN — Gastric Type

- Often found in branch ducts
- Lining epithelium has gastric foveolar phenotype
- Often with low-grade dysplasia
- High-grade dysplasia and invasive carcinoma can occur
- **Immunophenotype:**
  - Positive: CK7, MUC5AC
  - Negative: CK20, CDX2, MUC2, MUC1

---

## IPMN — Pancreatobiliary Type

- Usually involves main pancreatic duct
- More complex architecture with anastomosing papillae
- Composed of cuboidal cells with eosinophilic or amphophilic cytoplasm
- May or may not contain intracellular mucin
- Most have high-grade dysplasia within the lesion
- **Immunophenotype:**
  - Positive: CK7, MUC1, MUC5AC
  - Negative: CK20, CDX2, MUC2

---

## Figure 59.6 — Histopathology of IPMN and Variants

- **A:** Intestinal-type IPMN in main pancreatic duct with associated invasive colloid carcinoma; CBD not involved
- **B:** Gastric-type IPMN with foveolar-type epithelium
- **C:** Intraductal oncocytic papillary neoplasm (IOPN) with papillary growth pattern and eosinophilic/oncocytic cytoplasm
- **D:** Intraductal tubulopapillary neoplasm (ITPN) with complex tubular and cribriform pattern, lack of intracellular mucin

---

## Adenocarcinoma Arising in IPMN

- Can be either colloid type or conventional PDAC type
- **Colloid type:** Associated with intestinal-type IPMN
- **Conventional PDAC type:** Commonly associated with pancreatobiliary-type or gastric-type IPMN
- Thorough examination and adequate sampling crucial to identify occult carcinoma
- Particularly important in large lesions or cysts with complex architecture

---

## Intraductal Oncocytic Papillary Neoplasm (IOPN)

- Considered a variant of intraductal cystic papillary neoplasm
- Unique pathologic and molecular characteristics
- Exophytic growth pattern with friable papillary projections into dilated pancreatic ducts
- Histologically: back-to-back papillary or cribriform complexes
- Lined by multilayered columnar cells
- Characteristic eosinophilic (oncocytic) and granular cytoplasm
- Focal mucin-containing neoplastic epithelium can be observed
- **Immunophenotype:**
  - Oncocytic cells: positive for MUC1, MUC6, Heppar-1
  - Mucin-containing goblet cells: positive for MUC2, MUC5AC

---

## Intraductal Tubulopapillary Neoplasm (ITPN)

- Least common pancreatic intraductal neoplasm
- Predominant tubule-forming neoplasia with PD epithelial phenotype
- Lack of mucin production
- Macroscopically: more solid, less cystic appearance
- Intraductal growth may be difficult to recognize
- Microscopically: tightly packed tubules forming cribriform-appearing nests
- Tumor cells: cuboidal with scant eosinophilic or amphophilic cytoplasm
- Foci of necrosis and high-grade dysplasia common
- Invasive carcinoma identified in 70% of reported cases
- **Immunophenotype:**
  - Positive: CK7, MUC1, MUC6
  - Negative: MUC2, MUC5AC

---

## Intraductal Neoplasms — Molecular Biology and Genetics

- **IPMN:**
  - KRAS mutations: 60%–80%
  - GNAS mutations: 50%–70% (particularly intestinal phenotype)
  - RNF43 mutations: approximately 50%
  - GNAS mutation appears unique to IPMN (KRAS also common in PDAC)
- **IOPN:**
  - No defining genomic alterations in most cases
  - Recurrent mutations of ERBB4, ARHGAP26, ASXL1, EPHA8 identified in some cases
- **ITPN:**
  - Alterations in chromatin remodeling genes: MLL1-3, BAP1
  - PI3K pathway genes

---

## Mucinous Cystic Neoplasm (MCN) — Definition

- Cystic lesions of the pancreas
- Lined by mucin-producing neoplastic epithelium
- Can exhibit low-grade to high-grade dysplasia
- Noninvasive MCN = mucinous cystadenoma
- With invasion = mucinous cystadenocarcinoma

---

## MCN — Epidemiology and Clinical Features

- Occurs almost exclusively in women (> 98%)
- Mean onset age: 48 years
- Patients with mucinous cystadenocarcinoma are 5–10 years older on average
  - Suggests potential malignant progression from mucinous cystadenoma
- Majority located in body and tail of pancreas (> 98%)
- Radiographically: thick-walled cystic lesions without communication with pancreatic ducts
- Cystic fluid from preoperative aspiration shows elevated CEA levels
  - Helps distinguish MCN from nonmucinous cystic lesions
  - Serous cystadenoma, cystic neuroendocrine tumor, solid pseudopapillary neoplasm

---

## MCN — Prognosis

- Noninvasive MCN: favorable prognosis
  - 5-year survival: 100%
- Invasive mucinous cystadenocarcinoma: depends on pathologic stage
  - Tumor size and metastatic status
  - Estimated 5-year survival: 26%

---

## MCN — Pathologic Features

- Median diameter: approximately 6 cm
- Cyst wall fibrotic with peripheral calcifications ("egg-shell calcifications")
- MCNs with invasive carcinoma are reportedly larger
- Cyst lining relatively smooth in low-grade MCNs
- Irregularities (papillary projections, nodules) may be present in high-grade MCNs or mucinous cystadenocarcinoma
- Cyst can be unilocular or multilocular
- Contains thick mucin or necrotic debris

---

## MCN — Microscopic Features

- Typical MCN lined by tall columnar cells with abundant apical intracellular mucin
- Cyst wall may be denuded and lack epithelial lining
- Epithelium may be cuboidal and devoid of intracellular mucin
- **Defining features:**
  - Subepithelial spindle cell-rich, ovarian-like stroma
  - Nests of epithelioid cells resembling luteinized cells within stroma
- Density of ovarian-like stroma varies:
  - More cellular in younger patients
  - Less cellular in postmenopausal patients
  - Larger tumors tend to have less dense stroma

---

## Figure 59.7 — Mucinous Cystic Neoplasm (MCN)

- **A:** Gross photo of MCN with a unilocular cyst in the tail of pancreas without involvement of pancreatic duct
- **B:** Low-grade MCN lined by a single layer of tall columnar mucinous epithelium overlying dense ovarian-like stroma
- **C:** Ovarian-like stroma immunoreactive to estrogen receptor

---

## MCN — Grading

**Low-grade MCN:**
- Maintains cellular polarity
- Minimal nuclear stratification
- Mild to moderate cytologic atypia

**High-grade MCN:**
- Increased architectural complexity
- Cribriform and branching epithelium
- Budding papillae
- Loss of cellular polarity
- Significant cytologic atypia
- Frequent mitotic activity

---

## MCN — Invasive Carcinoma

- When invasive carcinoma is present, it recapitulates the phenotype of PDAC
- Includes:
  - Conventional tubular type adenocarcinoma
  - Adenosquamous carcinoma
  - Undifferentiated carcinoma with osteoclast-like giant cells

---

## MCN — Immunophenotype

- Neoplastic epithelium is predominantly of the pancreatobiliary type
- Exhibits pancreatobiliary immunophenotype
  - Reactivity to CK7 and CEA
- Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma expresses MUC1
- May lose nuclear SMAD4 expression
- Ovarian-like stromal cells:
  - Positive for estrogen and progesterone receptors
  - Luteinized cells immunoreactive to α-inhibin and calretinin

---

## MCN — Molecular Biology and Genetics

- Malignant epithelium harbors activating KRAS mutations in codon 12
- RNF43 gene alterations in 50%–66% of cases

---

## Serous Cystic Tumors — Introduction

- Exact pathogenesis not known
- Abnormal VHL/HIF pathway regulation in cells of centroacinar origin postulated as potential tumor cytogenesis
- Vast majority are benign
- Synonymous terminology with serous cystadenoma
- **Classification:**
  - Microcystic serous adenoma (most common)
  - Oligocystic serous adenoma
  - Solid serous adenoma
  - VHL syndrome-associated serous cystic adenoma
  - Mixed serous-neuroendocrine neoplasm
- Rare cases of serous cystadenocarcinoma (1%–3%)
- No specific morphologic criteria or molecular alterations characterizing malignant transformation
- Strict criteria for serous cystadenocarcinoma: presence of distant metastasis (< 0.2% of cases)

---

## Serous Cystadenoma — Epidemiology

- Accounts for 1%–2% of all pancreatic neoplasms
- 10%–16% of operations for pancreatic cystic lesions
- Most discovered incidentally by abdominal imaging
- Typically identified in age group 50–60 years (mean age 58)
- Female predominance (7:3)
- Patients may have nonspecific symptoms secondary to local mass effect
- More than 50% are asymptomatic

---

## Serous Cystadenoma — Clinical Features

- CT scan: well-circumscribed, multinodular cystic or microcystic mass
- Characteristic central scar with sunburst calcification pattern in approximately 30% of cases
- Tumor does not communicate with PD system
- Prognosis generally excellent
- Surgical resection almost always curative
- Radiographic observation considered appropriate for asymptomatic tumors after diagnosis

---

## Serous Cystadenoma — Pathologic Features

- Most commonly located in body or tail of pancreas (> 50%)
- Solitary tumor
- When associated with germline VHL gene alterations: multifocal lesions throughout entire pancreas
- Size varies; can be relatively large (up to 25 cm)
- **Microcystic variant:**
  - Well demarcated
  - Numerous minute cysts (1–2 mm)
  - Sponge-like texture
  - Calcifications may be observed in central scar
- **Macrocystic (oligocystic) type:**
  - Lacks central scar
  - Larger cysts (1–3 cm)
  - Unilocular or multilocular
- **Solid-type serous cystadenoma:** No cystic formation
- Serous cystadenomas do not usually communicate with PD system

---

## Figure 59.8 — Serous Cystadenoma

- **A:** Gross photo of serous cystadenoma with numerous minute cysts
- **B:** Microscopically, cysts lined by a single layer of cuboidal epithelium with clear cytoplasm and homogeneously hyperchromatic nuclei
- **C:** Co-existing serous cystadenoma (upper right) and neuroendocrine tumors (lower left) in a case of von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome

---

## Serous Cystadenoma — Microscopic Features

- Cysts lined by a single layer of nonmucinous, cuboidal epithelium
- Sharp cell borders
- Glycogen-containing clear cytoplasm
- Homogeneously hyperchromatic, round nuclei
- Distinctive capillary-rich network underlies tumor epithelium
- Nuclear atypia and mitotic activity uncommon
- Cytoplasm and cyst contents devoid of mucin and mucin-related glycoproteins/oncoproteins
  - Monoclonal CEA, CA125, CA19.9, MUC1
- This feature helps establish preoperative diagnosis

---

## Serous Cystadenoma — VHL Association

- Associated with VHL disease in 50%–90% of cases
- Usually presents as multifocal lesions throughout entire pancreas (diffuse serous cystadenoma)
- Can occur in microcystic or macrocystic form
- No significant morphologic distinction between sporadic and familial VHL-associated serous cystadenoma
- Neuroendocrine neoplasms can also develop in VHL disease:
  - 10%–17% of PanNET
  - 70% of neuroendocrine microadenomas
- Serous and neuroendocrine tumors can exist independently or intermingle
  - Mixed serous-neuroendocrine phenotype

---

## Serous Cystadenocarcinoma

- Unequivocal examples exceedingly rare (< 0.2%)
- Require evidence of distant metastasis (often to liver)
- Large tumors may exhibit locally aggressive features:
  - Direct extension or adhesion to adjacent organs/structures
  - Including liver
- Do not fulfill typical definition of malignancy

---

## Serous Tumors — Immunophenotype

- Recapitulate centroacinar cells in histopathology and immunophenotype
- Express:
  - Low molecular weight and broad-spectrum cytokeratins
  - EMA
  - MUC6
  - Inhibin

---

## Serous Tumors — Molecular Biology and Genetics

- VHL gene alterations account for both familial and sporadic serous cystic tumors
- Somatic VHL mutations at 3p25.3: 50% of cases
- Loss of heterozygosity of 3p: 90% of cases
- Allelic loss of chromosome 10p reported in 50% of serous cystadenomas

---

## Lymphoepithelial Cyst (LEC)

- Benign unilocular or multilocular lesions
- Lined by squamous epithelium
- Surrounding cuff of lymphocytes in cyst wall
- Rare: less than 1% of all pancreatic cystic lesions
- Pathogenesis unknown
- **Hypothetical etiologies:**
  - Development from squamous metaplasia of pancreatic ducts
  - Derivation from epithelial remnants in lymph nodes
  - Displacement of branchial cysts and fusion with pancreas during embryogenesis
  - Form of teratoma

---

## LEC — Epidemiology and Clinical Features

- Strong male preponderance (male to female ratio 3–4:1)
- Mean age: 56 years
- About half present incidentally
- Remaining associated with nonspecific symptoms
- Preoperative differential diagnosis includes:
  - Serous cystadenoma
  - MCN
  - IPMN
  - Pseudocyst
- Mean size at presentation: 4.7 cm
- Well circumscribed without communication with pancreatic ducts
- Sharply demarcated from adjacent normal pancreas

---

## LEC — Pathologic Features

- Cyst filled with chalky keratin debris
- Inner cyst wall smooth to granular
- Most lined by keratinized squamous epithelium
- Nonkeratinizing squamous epithelium, transitional epithelium, and flat cuboidal epithelium can be present
- Lining epithelium may exhibit reactive atypia secondary to inflammation
- Dysplasia is absent
- Layer of lymphoid stroma with varying thickness immediately beneath squamous epithelium
- May have germinal center formation

---

## Figure 59.9 — Lymphoepithelial Cyst (LEC)

- **A:** Gross photo of LEC filled with chalky keratin debris
- **B:** LEC lined by keratinized squamous epithelium overlying lymphoid tissue; keratin debris present in cyst content

---

## Neuroendocrine Tumors of the Pancreas — Historical Background

- Islet cell tumor first recognized in autopsy specimen by Nicholls in 1902
- After discovery of glucose regulatory function of insulin by Banting and Best et al. in 1921:
  - Insulinoma derived from β-cell of islet reported in 1924
- Virginia K. Franz at Columbia University described glucagonoma in detail in 1940
  - First one-stage pancreaticoduodenectomy specimen obtained by Allan Whipple
  - Production of glucagon confirmed only after radioimmunoassay became available in 1966
- Other functional islet tumors documented:
  - Gastrinoma associated with MEN-1 syndrome
  - VIPoma associated with Verner-Morrison syndrome
- Nonfunctional PanNET initially designated as "endocrine-inactive islet cell tumors"

---

## PanNEN — WHO 2019 Classification

1. **Pancreatic neuroendocrine microadenoma** (< 5 mm)
2. **Well-differentiated PanNET**
   - Nonfunctional
   - Functional (with clinical evidence of hormone release)
   - Insulinoma, glucagonoma, gastrinoma, VIPoma
3. **Poorly differentiated pancreatic NEC (PanNEC)**
   - Small cell and large cell PanNEC
   - Considered a variant carcinoma (discussed with PDAC)

---

## Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Microadenoma

- Arbitrarily designated by size: smaller than 5 mm
- Considered a precursor neoplasm of well-differentiated PanNET
- Particularly in setting of hereditary conditions and functional PanNETs
- Numerous microadenomas of varying sizes can be seen in background
- Before they are large enough (> 5 mm) to be designated as PanNETs
- **Common issue:** Distinguishing enlarged islet or aggregate of islets from microadenoma
- Normal pancreatic islets made up of two predominant endocrine cell populations:
  - Glucagon-producing α-cells
  - Insulin-producing β-cells
- α-cell and β-cell distribution delineated by immunohistochemical stains for glucagon and insulin

---

## Figure 59.10 — Microadenoma vs. Islet Cell Hyperplasia

- Nonneoplastic islet aggregate (**A**) with normal central insulin (**B**) and peripheral glucagon (**C**) distribution on immunostains
- Pancreatic neuroendocrine microadenoma (**D**) lacks insulin expression (**E**) and has clonal production of glucagon (**F**)

---

## Microadenoma vs. Normal Islet

- Regardless of size of islet:
  - If glucagon and insulin distributions reveal a normal pattern → not a neoplasm
- Microadenoma represents a neoplastic process:
  - Hormone production is either clonal with abnormal distribution
  - Or derives from random expression of multiple pancreatic or nonpancreatic peptide hormones

---

## Islet Aggregation and Nesidioblastosis

- Aggregation of islets commonly seen in atrophic pancreas
  - Secondary to duct obstruction by tumor or diffuse CP
- Islet aggregates sometimes considered synonymous with "nesidioblastosis" — misconception
- George F. Laidlaw coined term nesidioblastosis in 1938
  - Greek words for islet (nesidion) and builder (blastos)
  - Emphasized cells differentiate and bud from PD epithelium to form new islet tissue
  - Believed to be pathogenic mechanism of congenital hyperinsulinemia
- In 1970s–1980s, nesidioblastosis synonymous with congenital hyperinsulinemia
- 1995: Genetic basis identified as inactivating mutation in subunit forming β-cell plasma membrane ATP-dependent potassium channel
- Malfunction, not proliferation, of β-cells accountable for hyperinsulinemia
- Preferred terminology: idiopathic hyperinsulinism of infant or adult
- Term nesidioblastosis not recommended for hyperinsulinism or islet aggregates in atrophic pancreas

---

## PanNET — Classification

- Historically classified as:
  1. Functional NETs with clinical evidence of hormone release and associated symptoms
  2. Nonfunctional NETs
- Further stratified by tumor differentiation and tumor grade
- Two categories sometimes used interchangeably — generated confusion
- Best classified as:
  - Well-differentiated PanNET
  - Poorly differentiated PanNEC

---

## PanNET — Pathologic Features (1)

- Vary in size; solid and fleshy appearance
- Characteristic pathologic features of neuroendocrine lineage
- Morphologically resemble nonneoplastic counterpart (neuroendocrine cells of islet)
- Tumor cells contain neuroendocrine secretory granules in cytoplasm
- Diffuse and strong immunoreactivity to neuroendocrine markers:
  - Chromogranin-A
  - Synaptophysin
- Most PanNETs are low- to intermediate-grade (WHO G1 and G2)
- Can rarely progress to high-grade (WHO G3)
  - Mitotic activity > 20 per 10 high-power fields
  - Ki67 proliferative index > 20%

---

## PanNET — Pathologic Features (2)

- High-grade component in PanNET usually not homogenous
- Lower-grade counterpart often observed in resection specimens or specimens from different sites
  - Primary vs. metastasis
- G3 PanNET rarely seen at initial presentation without obvious progression
- Distinguishing high-grade PanNET (WHO G3) from PanNEC in small biopsies can be challenging
- Poorly differentiated PanNECs:
  - Do not resemble neuroendocrine cells of islet
  - Rarely resemble any nonneoplastic epithelial cell counterparts
  - High-grade cytologic features
  - Only partial expression of neuroendocrine markers
- PanNEC does not represent genetic progression from lower-grade PanNET

---

## PanNET — Macroscopic Features

- Most sharply demarcated from adjacent pancreatic parenchyma
- Or encapsulated
- Small tumors: homogeneous and fleshy in consistency
- Partially cystic tumors not uncommon (secondary to degenerative changes)
- Large PanNETs: often multiloculated or multinodular
- Can exhibit gross invasion into:
  - Peripancreatic tissues
  - Mesentery
  - Adjacent organs (stomach, duodenum, colon, spleen)
- Vascular invasion may be grossly evident (particularly splenic vein)
- Most do not involve pancreatic duct
- Variant of serotonin-producing PanNET described:
  - Arises from pancreatic duct with associated fibrosis
  - Similar to mesenteric fibrosis seen in NETs of small intestine
  - May generate clinical impression of ductal adenocarcinoma (duct obstruction and jaundice)

---

## Figure 59.11 — Well-Differentiated PanNET

- **A:** Gross photo of PanNET with well-circumscribed, fleshy-appearing lesion
- **B:** PanNET showing trabecular pattern with low-grade cytologic features

---

## PanNET — Microscopic Features

- Characteristic histologic patterns:
  - Loosely cohesive
  - Nested
  - Trabecular/gyriform
  - Hyaline vascular architecture
  - Clear cell change
  - Pleomorphic type
- Groups of neoplastic cells separated by enriched and delicate vessels
- Most are hypercellular and stroma-poor
- Tumor cells: copious granular eosinophilic or amphophilic cytoplasm
- Usually polygonal without distinct cell borders
- Nucleus centrally or peripherally located (latter → plasmacytoid appearance)
- Nuclei usually uniform in size and shape
- Characteristically finely stippled appearance (better appreciated in well-fixed tissue)

---

## PanNET — High-Grade Transformation

- May be morphologically subtle on routine histopathology evaluation
- Immunostain of Ki67 can be helpful
- Figure 59.12:
  - **A:** Hematoxylin-and-eosin-stained PanNET with subtle morphologic alterations
  - **B:** Ki67 immunostain showing high proliferative index

---

## Figure 59.12 — PanNET with High-Grade Transformation

- **A:** H&E-stained PanNET with subtle morphologic alterations
- **B:** Ki67 immunostain highlighting high proliferative activity

---

## PanNET — Morphologic Variants

- Uncommon morphologic variants:
  - Oncocytic phenotype
  - Clear cell change
  - Should be distinguished from renal cell carcinoma (most common metastatic malignancy in pancreas)
- **Pleomorphic PanNETs:**
  - Marked nuclear atypia
  - Can be confused with poorly differentiated or undifferentiated ductal adenocarcinomas
  - Despite bizarre cytologic features, most do not demonstrate increased proliferative activity
  - Do not correlate with unfavorable outcome

---

## Hereditary PanNET Syndromes

**Four established hereditary associations:**
1. MEN-1/4
2. VHL disease
3. Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)
4. Tuberous sclerosis (TSC)

- All inherited as autosomal dominant disorders
- Frequencies of PanNET:
  - High in MEN1 (30%–80%)
  - High in VHL (17%)
  - Extremely rare in NF1 and TSC
- NF1-associated duodenal and ampullary somatostatinoma more common

**Fifth hereditary PanNET:**
- Mahvash disease
- Autosomal recessive
- Homozygous or biallelic heterozygous mutation of gene encoding glucagon receptor
- Patients present with asymptomatic hyperglucagonemia
- Develop multiple glucagonomas
- Penetrance 100% by 60 years of age (based on limited case reports)

**Insulinomatosis:**
- Not associated with MEN-1/4
- Molecular and genetic mechanisms remain to be delineated

---

## Hereditary PanNET — Pathologic Relevance

- Precursor microadenomas present in:
  - MEN-1 (predominantly insulin- and glucagon-producing in pancreas; gastrin-producing in duodenum)
  - Mahvash disease (glucagon-producing)
- Microscopic finding of spectrum of abnormal islets with varying sizes in background
  - Should raise possibility of one of these hereditary conditions
- Multiple PanNETs often observed in MEN-1, VHL, and Mahvash disease
- Challenge in management when patient is symptomatic
  - Source of hormone production can be from one of several tumors
- Patients with VHL can also develop serous cystadenomas that coexist with PanNETs

---

## Figure 59.13 — Hereditary PanNET

- **A:** Hereditary PanNET with abnormal islets of varying sizes and neuroendocrine microadenoma and PanNET
- **B:** von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) with serous cystadenoma (lower right) and co-existing well-differentiated neuroendocrine neoplasm (upper left)

---

## PanNET — Molecular Biology and Genetics (1)

- Hereditary syndromes account for less than 10% of PanNETs
- Germline mutations in DNA damage repair genes (CHEK2, MUTYH) identified in 17% of sporadic cases without apparent familial association
- Early cytogenetic and molecular genetic studies identified many chromosomal alterations
  - Result of progressive accumulation associated with clinical tumor stage and disease progression
- Deletions more frequently detected in primary PanNET
- Increased copy numbers seen in metastatic tumors
- Activation of oncogenes does not appear to play major role in PanNET development

---

## PanNET — Molecular Biology and Genetics (2)

- Advances in NGS enabled genome-wide analyses
- Highlighted molecular heterogeneity of disease
- Many genes implicated in PDAC development not affected in PanNETs
  - KRAS2, TP53, p16/CDKN2A, SMAD4 usually not mutated
- Even in absence of TP53 mutation, impaired p53 pathway evident:
  - Amplifications of negative regulators of p53: MDM2, MDM4, WIP1
- MEN1 (44%) and DAXX/ATRX (43%) frequently mutated in sporadic PanNETs
- DAXX and ATRX mutations are mutually exclusive
- More than 20% of tumors harbor either DAXX or ATRX and MEN1 mutations
- Collectively, about 60% of PanNETs carry MEN1/DAXX/ATRX mutations

---

## PanNET — Molecular Correlations

- Genes affect epigenetic landscape, epigenome
  - DNA methylation, histone modification, posttranscriptional regulation
  - Ultimately gene expression
- Likely plays critical role in pathogenesis of PanNET
- PanNETs with MEN1/DAXX/ATRX mutant genotype as a group:
  - Correlate with worse clinical prognosis than tumors carrying wild-type alleles
- Different gene expression profiles:
  - MEN1/DAXX/ATRX-mutant PanNETs exhibit gene signatures of islet α-cell lineage
  - MEN1/DAXX/ATRX wild-type PanNETs more heterogeneous in gene expressions
- Findings suggest PanNETs may be further characterized into different subtypes based on cell lineage and molecular genotype
- Mutations in PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway occur in 14.7% of PanNETs
  - Involves vital cellular processes of cell cycle progression, angiogenesis, DNA repair, epigenetic regulation, gene expression
- Treatment with mTOR inhibitor everolimus has shown improved survival in subset of patients with advanced PanNETs

---

## Tumors with Acinar Differentiation — Overview

- Acinar cell cystadenoma (acinar cyst transformation)
- Acinar cell carcinoma
- Pancreatoblastoma

---

## Acinar Cell Cystadenoma

- Considered a non-neoplastic cystic lesion
- Lined by mixed acinar and ductal epithelium
- Proposed etiology: obstruction or metaplastic process
- Exact incidence unknown (less than 50 cases reported)
- May be underrecognized or misdiagnosed
- Can occur at any age with female predominance (3:1)
- Lesions vary significantly in size (from less than 1 cm to 20 cm)
- Mean size: 5.8 cm
- Clinically evident or incidental microscopic finding
- Patients with large acinar cell cystadenoma can experience mass-related clinical symptoms
- All reported cases clinically benign without evidence of recurrence or malignant transformation
- No pathologic association with acinar cell carcinoma or pancreatoblastoma

---

## Acinar Cell Cystadenoma — Pathologic Features

- Radiographically: 1.5 cm to 17.9 cm in greatest dimension
- Multicentricity common
- Can form unilocular or multilocular cysts
- Smooth, thin inner wall with clear fluid
- Do not communicate with pancreatic ducts
- Microscopically: cysts of varying sizes separated by either atrophic pancreatic parenchyma or incomplete fibrotic septa
- Some cysts filled with eosinophilic proteinaceous material
- Lined by one or two layers of simple cuboidal epithelium
- Pale eosinophilic or granulated cytoplasm
- Acinar differentiation appreciated when granular and intense eosinophilic cytoplasm is apically located
- Nuclei basally oriented
- Presence of intervening columnar epithelium with ductal differentiation can create diagnostic challenge
- Differential diagnosis: serous cystadenoma, squamous cysts of pancreatic ducts, retention cyst, low-grade PanIN, variants of intraductal papillary neoplasm

---

## Figure 59.14 — Tumors with Acinar Differentiation

- **A:** Acinar cystadenoma lined by mixed acinar and ductal type epithelium
- **B:** Acinar cell carcinoma with acinar architecture and polarized apical eosinophilic and granular cytoplasm
- **C:** Pancreatoblastoma with a squamoid nest

---

## Acinar Cell Cystadenoma — Immunohistochemistry

- Immunostains for cytokeratin, including CK7, are positive
- Reveal the ductal differentiation of cyst-lining cells
- Cells with apparent acinar differentiation:
  - Positive for periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain with resistance to diastase
  - Stain positive for pancreatic enzymes (trypsin and chymotrypsin) by immunohistochemistry

---

## Acinar Cell Cystadenoma — Malignant Transformation

- Rare cases of malignant transformation to cystadenocarcinoma reported
- Diagnosis based on combination of morphologic features and distant metastasis
- Microscopic findings include recognizable acinar cell cystadenoma with increased architectural complexity resembling acinar cell carcinoma
- Most reported cases had liver or peritoneal metastasis
- Mean survival: 14.3 months

---

## Acinar Cell Cystadenoma — Molecular Biology

- No pathogenic gene alterations identified in acinar cell cystadenoma
- Some studies reported random X-chromosome inactivation

---

## Acinar Cell Carcinoma — Definition

- Malignant epithelial neoplasm derived from acinar cells of the pancreas
- Subtypes include:
  - Acinar cell cystadenocarcinoma
  - Mixed acinar-NEC
  - Mixed acinar-neuroendocrine-ductal carcinoma
  - Mixed acinar-ductal combination
- These subtypes appear to share the same cytogenetic background

---

## Acinar Cell Carcinoma — Epidemiology

- Male sex predominance (2:1)
- Accounts for less than 2% of pancreatic neoplasms in adults
- Accounts for 15% in children
- Age of onset: 60 to 70 years of age (range 2–88 years)
- Although uncommon, up to 6% of acinar cell carcinomas can occur in children
- Majority of cases are sporadic
- Rare cases diagnosed in association with:
  - Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP)
  - Lynch syndrome
  - Carney's complex

---

## Acinar Cell Carcinoma — Clinical Features

- Symptoms usually related to mass effect
- When associated with disseminated metastasis:
  - Subcutaneous fat necrosis
  - Polyarthralgia
  - Due to hypersecretion of pancreatic enzymes (lipase) from tumor cells
- Alpha-fetal protein may be present at increased levels in young patients
- Usually appears as well-demarcated, large enhancing mass on radiographic studies
- Median survival: 19 months
- 5-year survival: approximately 25%

---

## Acinar Cell Carcinoma — Pathologic Features

- Average size at presentation: approximately 9 cm
- Fleshy and homogeneous appearance
- Friable consistency because of hypercellular nature
- Focal necrosis and cystic change may occur (large-size-associated degeneration)
- Microscopically: characteristically hypercellular with minimal thin fibrous septa
- Lacks stromal desmoplasia
- At low magnification: tumor cells arranged in sheets and large nests with lobulated growth pattern
- Acinar pattern of small units most characteristic
  - Resemblance to normal pancreatic acini
  - Minute luminal spaces or solid central eosinophilic rosettes
- Other histologic patterns: solid, glandular, trabecular
  - Can bear resemblance to well-differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor
- Less common histology subtypes: oncocytic, clear, spindle, and pleomorphic variants
- Tumor cells usually monotonous with mild to moderate nuclear atypia and prominent nucleoli
- Tumor mitotic activity variable but usually increased
- Apically located abundant eosinophilic zymogen granules in cytoplasm
  - Highly suggestive of acinar cell carcinoma
  - Not always histologically appreciated

---

## Acinar Cell Carcinoma — Diagnosis

- Definitive diagnosis requires documentation of pancreatic enzyme production in tumor cells
- Zymogen granules stain positively with PAS with resistance to diastase
- Immunohistochemical staining of trypsin and/or chymotrypsin has highest degree of sensitivity
- C-terminal portion of BCL10 is also specific in identifying acinar differentiation by recognizing pancreatic lipase
- β-catenin nuclear reactivity observed in about 10% of cases

---

## Mixed Acinar Cell Carcinoma

- Defined as having greater than 30% of each line of cell differentiation
- Most encountered type: mixed acinar-NEC
- In most cases, two cell types are intermingled without morphologically distinct acinar and neuroendocrine components
- Diagnosis usually established based on co-expression of acinar and neuroendocrine markers by immunohistochemistry
- Mixed acinar-NEC should be regarded as a subtype of acinar cell carcinoma
  - Shares clinical and genomic characteristics with pure acinar cell carcinoma
- Mixed acinar-ductal carcinoma:
  - Usually has distinct component of gland-forming ductal adenocarcinoma
  - Uncommon
  - Associated with poor clinical outcome
- Combined line of cell differentiation may also include acinar-neuroendocrine-ductal carcinoma

---

## Acinar Cell Carcinoma — Molecular Genetics

- No consistent genetic alterations in most cases
- Small subset carry SMAD4, CDKN2A, and CDKN2B mutations
- Abnormalities in APC/β-catenin pathway documented
- Mutations in APC and CTNNB1 genes each occur in less than 10% of cases
- APC gene loss (48% of cases) or promoter hypermethylation (56% of cases) may be more frequent
- BRAF and RAF1 gene rearrangements found in 23% of cases

---

## Pancreatoblastoma — Definition

- Malignant acinar cell neoplasm with distinct squamous nests
- Endocrine, ductal, and mesenchymal differentiation can also be uncommonly observed within tumor
- Prognosis more favorable in children than adults
- 5-year survival: 65% for those with resectable tumors
- 18% develop locoregional recurrence
- Distant metastasis (mostly to liver) associated with poor outcome

---

## Pancreatoblastoma — Epidemiology and Clinical Features

- Rare neoplasm in adults
- Accounts for 25% of pancreatic neoplasms in early childhood
- Median age: 4 to 5 years
- Most cases sporadic
- Association with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis reported
- Most common clinical presentation: palpable mass and associated symptoms
- Inappropriate ACTH secretion from tumor can cause Cushing syndrome (rare)
- Markedly elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) common in two-thirds of cases, particularly children

---

## Pancreatoblastoma — Pathologic Features

- Usually large solitary mass
- Mean diameter: 10 cm
- Focal necrosis and cystic change can occur secondary to degeneration
- Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome-associated pancreatoblastoma may be predominantly cystic
- Hypercellular neoplasm with lobulated growth pattern separated by fibrous septa
- Similar to acinar cell carcinoma:
  - Tumor cells with acinar differentiation form small units of acini
  - Polarized eosinophilic and granular cytoplasm
  - Tiny lumina in center
- Presence of squamoid nests is essential feature for diagnosis
  - Composed of epithelial cells with varying degree of squamous differentiation
  - With or without keratinization
- Heterologous stromal elements (bone and cartilage) may also be present

---

## Pancreatoblastoma — Immunohistochemistry

- Immunostaining for β-catenin should reveal nuclear pattern of reactivity in most cases
- Acinar component of tumor is positive for:
  - PAS with resistance to diastase
  - Pancreatic enzymes
  - BCL10

---

## Pancreatoblastoma — Molecular Biology and Genetics

- Loss of chromosome 11p occurs in more than 80% of:
  - Sporadic pancreatoblastomas
  - Cases of children with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
- APC pathway alterations involving CTNNB1 mutations present in 50% to 80% of pancreatoblastomas
  - Result in abnormal β-catenin nuclear labeling

---

## Solid Pseudopapillary Neoplasm (SPN) — Introduction

- Cell lineage unknown
- Striking predominance among females and young age distribution
  - Suggests potential hormonal effect
  - No apparent association with endocrine imbalances reported
- SPNs described in ovary and testis
- Suggested that cells giving rise to SPN occur in genital ridges and migrate to pancreas during embryogenesis

---

## SPN — Epidemiology and Clinical Features

- Accounts for 0.9% to 2.7% of all exocrine pancreatic neoplasms in adults
- Represents about 5% of all cystic pancreatic neoplasms
- Predominantly in young women (mean age 28 years; > 85% female)
- No apparent ethnic predilection
- When SPN occurs in men, age of onset usually 5 to 10 years older than women
- Low-grade malignant neoplasm
- Complete surgical resection curative in most cases
- Metastasis occurs in less than 15% of patients
  - Usually to liver or peritoneum
- Even with metastasis, patients usually have protracted clinical course
  - 10-year disease-specific survival rate: 96%
- Rare cases of highly aggressive SPNs reported
  - Transformation from conventional SPN to high-grade malignancy or carcinoma phenotype

---

## SPN — Pathologic Features (1)

- Grossly: well demarcated
- At presentation may be as large as 8 to 10 cm in diameter
- Solid appearance when small
- Cystic degeneration and intratumor hemorrhage common when tumor is large
- Calcifications may be present in septa or wall of tumor
- Microscopically: heterogeneous histologic pattern
- Various proportions of solid, cystic, and pseudopapillary structures
- Periphery of tumor may interweave with adjacent pancreatic parenchyma
  - Creating poorly defined margin
- Neoplastic cells round to oval
- Eosinophilic or vacuolated cytoplasm
- Often containing diastase-resistant PAS-positive hyaline globules

---

## SPN — Pathologic Features (2)

- Solid component:
  - May resemble well-differentiated PanNET or acinar cell carcinoma
  - Composed of uniform cells arranged in poorly or loosely cohesive pattern
  - Intertwined capillary vessels
- Pseudopapillary morphology:
  - Secondary to detachment of neoplastic cells distant from vessels
  - Leaving some tumor cells clinging to hyalinized or myxoid fibrovascular cords
- Nuclei of tumor cells: round to oval
- Often grooved or indented with finely dispersed chromatin
- Tumor mitotic activity: nil
- Lympho-vascular and perineural invasion: uncommon
- Areas with hemorrhage and cystic degeneration:
  - Foamy macrophages
  - Deposits of cholesterol crystals

---

## Figure 59.15 — Solid Pseudopapillary Neoplasm (SPN)

- **A:** Gross photo of a large SPN with degenerative changes
- **B:** Microscopic photo of SPN with prominent papillary structure

---

## SPN — Immunophenotype

- Distinctive immunophenotype helpful in differential diagnosis
- Morphologic mimics: well-differentiated PanNET and pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma
- Tumor cells characteristically reveal:
  - Nuclear or cytoplasmic immunoreactivity for β-catenin
  - Express vimentin
  - Progesterone receptors
  - CD10
  - Some less specific neuroendocrine markers (CD56, synaptophysin)
- Chromogranin (most specific neuroendocrine marker): negative in SPN
  - Important for differential diagnosis with PanNETs
- Pancreatic enzymes (trypsin, chymotrypsin): not expressed
  - Distinguishes SPN from pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma
- CD99: dot-like paranuclear expression pattern
- Tumor cells may show patchy reactivity to pan-cytokeratin or low-molecular-weight cytokeratin
- Often negative for cytokeratin
- Never reveal diffusely positive pattern

---

## SPN — Molecular Biology and Genetics

- Somatic activating mutations in exon 3 of CTNNB1 gene
- Involved in Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway
- Mutations prevent phosphorylation of β-catenin in cytoplasm
- Result in loss of membranous expression
- β-catenin translocated to nucleus

---

## Mesenchymal and Other Non-Epithelial Tumors — Introduction

- Primary mesenchymal or nonepithelial neoplasms of pancreas are rare
- Account for 1% to 2% of pancreatic tumors
- Pathologic classification similar to same neoplasms arising outside pancreas
- Can be either solid or cystic
- Distinguishing from more common epithelial neoplasms can be diagnostically challenging
  - Both clinically and radiographically

**Benign mesenchymal tumors:**
- Mature cystic teratoma
- Lymphangioma
- Schwannoma
- Ganglioneuroma
- Granular cell tumor
- Desmoid tumor
- Leiomyoma
- Lipoma
- Perivascular epithelioid cell tumor (PEComa)
- Paraganglioma

---

## Mature Cystic Teratoma

- Germ cell origin
- Commonly found in ovaries and testes
- May arise anywhere along path of germ cell migration during embryogenesis
- Usually along midline of body
- Pancreas is least common site
- Majority composed of ectodermal elements (hair follicles, sebaceous glands, skin)
- Also referred to as dermoid cysts
- Usually diagnosed in younger patients
- Mean age: 36 years (range 4 months to 74 years)
- Important to differentiate from mucinous neoplasms (MCN, IPMN)
  - Given potential for malignant transformation
- Difficulty in definitive preoperative diagnosis (particularly larger lesions > 3 cm)
  - Often leads to surgical resection

---

## Mature Cystic Teratoma — Pathologic Features

- Slow-growing
- Can be large at presentation
- Mean size: 7 to 8 cm (range 2–20 cm)
- Macroscopically: heterogeneous with solid and cystic areas
- Cystic contents may appear pasty
  - Containing hair, keratinous debris, sebaceous material
- Microscopically: cyst wall lined by epithelium
  - May be squamous, respiratory, or glandular
- All reported cases of pancreatic teratomas classified as mature and thus benign
- Complete sampling of resected specimen recommended
  - To exclude presence of any immature elements
- Prognosis excellent with complete resection
- Neither recurrence nor malignant transformation reported

---

## Lymphangioma

- Benign tumors arising from lymphatic system
- 95% of cases occur in neck/axilla
- Less than 5% occur in mesentery/retroperitoneum
- Pancreatic lymphangiomas account for less than 1% of all abdominal lymphangiomas
- May arise from pancreatic parenchyma or adjacent tissue
- Possible etiology: congenital lymphatic malformations lead to lymphatic obstruction and development of lymphangiectasia
- Symptoms vary, nonspecific, typically based on locoregional effects
- Reported in all age groups but more commonly in women

---

## Lymphangioma — Pathologic Features

- Macroscopically: cystic masses, usually multilocular
- Cysts may be interconnected (dilated lymphatic channels)
- Cysts contain chylous, serous, or serosanguineous fluid
- Microscopically: cystic or cavernous subtype
- Cyst walls lined with endothelial cells
- Composed of varying amounts of collagenous connective tissue, smooth muscle, focal adipose tissue, lymphocytes
- Lining endothelial cells immunoreactive to CD31 and D2-40
- Usually negative for CD34
- Negative for epithelial markers
- Differential diagnosis: pancreatic MCN, branch-duct IPMN, serous cystadenoma, retention cysts, pseudocysts, other solid tumors with cystic degeneration
- Diagnosis can be made when cystic fluid (EUS aspiration) has elevated triglyceride level (above 5000 mg/dL or 56.5 mmol/L)
- Cyst fluid should be tested for CEA to rule out epithelial lesions
- Generally benign but may be locally invasive
- Surgical excision curative; incomplete resection may result in recurrence

---

## Schwannoma

- Predominantly benign peripheral nerve sheath tumors
- Composed of Schwann cells
- Most are solitary
- Multiple schwannomas associated with neurofibromatosis type 2
- Pancreatic schwannoma extremely rare (only 37 reported cases in English literature)
- Typically occurs in adults
- Affects men and women equally
- Arise from autonomic sympathetic or parasympathetic nerves within pancreas
- Identified more often in head, body, and uncinate process
- Less frequently in tail of pancreas
- Slow-growing but may be large at diagnosis
- Average size: 9 cm (range 2–20 cm)
- Most common symptom: vague abdominal pain

---

## Schwannoma — Pathologic Features

- Macroscopically: well-circumscribed, round, firm, encapsulated masses
- Large tumors may have secondary degenerative alterations:
  - Cyst formation
  - Hemorrhage
  - Calcification
  - Yellowish xanthomatous change
- Histologically: intertwined hypercellular (Antoni-A) and hypocellular (Antoni-B) spindle cell neoplasm
- Lymphocytes may be present at periphery
- Hypocellular area can have myxoid changes
- Diffusely positive for S100 on immunohistochemistry
- Treatment: surgical resection
- Prognosis should mirror nonpancreatic primaries
- Presence of underlying neurofibromatosis adversely affects prognosis

---

## Ganglioneuroma

- Benign mesenchymal tumors
- Arise from sympathetic ganglion cells
- Consist of mature gangliocytes and stroma
- Pancreatic ganglioneuromas exceedingly rare
- May arise from peripancreatic sympathetic nerve fibers
- Symptoms related to mass effect on adjacent structures
- Most detected incidentally
- Average size at presentation: approximately 8 cm
- Tumors firm and well-circumscribed
- Although not usually encapsulated
- Microscopically: Schwann cells and variable amounts of mature ganglion cells
- Tumor cells immunoreactive to:
  - Neuron-specific enolase
  - Neurofilament protein
  - Synaptophysin
- Treatment: complete surgical resection
- Recurrence rare

---

## Granular Cell Tumor

- Benign nerve sheath origin
- Only rare cases in pancreas reported
- Clinical diagnosis may be challenging
- May mimic ductal adenocarcinoma
- Microscopically: characteristic eosinophilic granular cytoplasm
- Small and inconspicuous nuclei
- Definitive diagnosis established by tumor cells' positive immunoreactivity to S100

---

## Desmoid Tumor

- Locally aggressive mesenchymal tumors
- Typically associated with FAP and Gardner syndrome
- May occur sporadically or as result of trauma or surgery
- Ten cases of desmoid tumors of pancreas described over past several decades
- No metastatic potential
- Exhibit locally aggressive growth
- Invade adjacent structures
- Estimated morbidity: 10%
- Patients may be asymptomatic or have symptoms related to mass effect
- Complications associated with encasement of adjacent structures

---

## Desmoid Tumor — Pathologic Features

- Macroscopically: homogeneous, firm, white masses
- Usually have infiltrative borders
- Tumor can occasionally be cystic
- Composed of bland proliferative fibroblasts within collagen matrix
- Low-grade
- Lack pleomorphism, atypia, and significant mitotic activities
- Positive nuclear β-catenin immunoreactivity effective in distinguishing desmoid tumors from other spindle-cell neoplasms with fibroblastic and myoblastic differentiation
- Differential diagnosis: solitary fibrous tumor, GI stromal tumor (GIST), low-grade sarcoma
- All have characteristic immunophenotype that does not overlap with desmoid tumors
- Surgery is mainstay treatment
- Achievement of clear resection margins may be challenging due to infiltrative growth pattern
- Risk of recurrence: 20% to 75%
- Higher rate in patients with FAP or Gardner syndrome

---

## Leiomyoma

- Benign smooth muscle tumors
- Usually arise in organs composed primarily of smooth muscle
- Primary leiomyoma of pancreas exceedingly rare
- Likely arises from smooth muscle wall of blood vessels
- Microscopically: spindle cells with characteristic blunt-ended and cigar-shaped nuclei
- Eosinophilic cytoplasm
- Diffusely positive for smooth muscle actin and desmin by immunohistochemistry
- Differential diagnosis includes other mesenchymal tumors of pancreas (e.g., leiomyosarcoma)

---

## Lipoma

- Benign mesenchymal tumors composed of mature adipose tissue
- Uncommon in pancreas
- Pancreatic lipomatosis or diffuse fatty change of pancreas can be seen in:
  - Cystic fibrosis
  - Schwachman-Diamond syndrome
  - CP
  - Obesity
  - DM
  - May be age-related
- Differential diagnosis: other fat-containing neoplasms
  - Cystic teratoma
  - Liposarcoma
  - Fibrolipoma
  - Lipoblastoma
- Grossly: well-circumscribed fatty lesions
- Given classic imaging findings, histologic confirmation may not be necessary
- Microscopically: mature adipocytes with delicate fibrous septa and thin collagen capsule
- Lipomatosis and lipomas can be observed and managed conservatively
- Presence of solid nodules, thick septa, calcification, or rapid growth raises concern for malignant transformation to liposarcoma or other malignancies

---

## Perivascular Epithelioid Cell Tumor (PEComa)

- Also known as angiomyolipoma
- Mesenchymal tumor arising from perivascular epithelioid smooth muscle cells with clear cytoplasm
- PEComa of pancreas very rare (few cases described)
- Strong female predominance
- Some cases related to genetic alteration in tuberous sclerosis gene complex
- Usually located in head and body of pancreas
- Grossly: well-circumscribed tumors
- Average size: 2.5 cm
- May demonstrate hemorrhage or cystic degeneration
- Microscopically: nests of large low-grade epithelioid cells
- Eosinophilic or clear (glycogen-rich) cytoplasm
- Macrovesicular fat may be present (uncommon)
- Glycogen-rich clear cells positive for PAS and diastase sensitive
- Co-express smooth muscle actin (SMA) and melanocytic markers (HMB-45, Melan-A)
- Negative for cytokeratin by immunohistochemistry
- Differential diagnosis: other cellular epithelial tumors of pancreas
  - Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor
  - Uncommon variants of adenocarcinoma expressing cytokeratin and other lineage-specific markers

---

## Paraganglioma

- Tumors arising from extra-adrenal paraganglia
- Nests of specialized neural crest cells dispersed along sympathetic ganglia and plexuses throughout body
- Retroperitoneal paragangliomas arising in peripancreatic location can manifest as primary pancreatic neoplasms
- Incidence same for men and women
- Most often detected in patients between ages 42 and 85 years
- Most retroperitoneal/pancreatic paragangliomas are nonfunctional
- Discovered incidentally or in patients with abdominal pain or palpable abdominal mass
- Functioning paragangliomas can cause symptoms of catecholamine excess:
  - Palpitations
  - Headache
  - Sweating
  - Hypertension
- Associated with elevated urine and plasma metanephrine and normetanephrine levels

---

## Paraganglioma — Pathologic Features

- All share similar pathologic features regardless of site of origin
- Grossly: well-marginated fleshy and tan-brown mass
- Microscopically: typical zellballen arrangement
  - Variably sized nests of tumor cells
  - Entwined reticular vascular network
- Tumor cells contain abundant granular amphophilic cytoplasm and eccentric nuclei
- Tumor nests surrounded by delicate sustentacular cells
- Immunohistochemistry:
  - Tumor cells express chromogranin and synaptophysin
  - Sustentacular cells positive for S100
  - Immunostains for cytokeratin should be negative in tumor cells
  - Distinguishes paraganglioma from epithelial neuroendocrine neoplasm
- Metastasis rarely occurs
- No morphologic criteria that can unequivocally define malignancy
- Preoperative diagnosis can be challenging
- Differential diagnosis: other hyper-enhancing tumors of pancreas on CT
  - Well-differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors
- When dealing with neuroendocrine neoplasm in small biopsies:
  - Immunostain of cytokeratin should be performed in addition to neuroendocrine markers
  - Diagnosis of paraganglioma (negative for cytokeratin) requires preoperative preparation to prevent intraoperative hypertensive crisis

---

## Malignant Mesenchymal and Nonepithelial Tumors — Overview

- Group consists primarily of sarcomas resembling soft-tissue counterparts
- 10% of sarcomas arise in retroperitoneum
- When occurring in peripancreatic retroperitoneal space, can infiltrate pancreas and simulate primary pancreatic neoplasm
- Less commonly occur primarily within pancreas
- Sarcomas represent 0.1% of all pancreatic malignancies
- Classification and clinical behavior similar to same neoplasms arising outside pancreas

**Types:**
- Leiomyosarcoma
- Liposarcoma
- Primitive neuroectodermal tumor (PNET) and extraosseous Ewing sarcoma (EES)
- Extragastrointestinal stromal tumor (E-GIST)
- Solitary fibrous tumor (SFT)
- Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT)

---

## Leiomyosarcoma

- Very rare
- Most common primary sarcoma of pancreas
- Affects women more often than men
- Mean age: mid-50s
- Tumor can be large (some as big as 30 cm)
- Large tumors usually associated with:
  - Cystic degeneration
  - Hemorrhage
  - Necrosis
- Microscopically: spindled tumor cells arranged in long and storiform fascicles
- Marked nuclear pleomorphism
- Eosinophilic cytoplasm
- Neoplastic cells immunoreactive to muscle markers SMA and desmin
- Differential diagnosis: primary undifferentiated/sarcomatous carcinoma of pancreas
  - May show partial expression of muscle markers
  - Should have some expression for cytokeratin (although reactivity can be focal)

---

## Liposarcoma

- Affects middle-aged or older patients
- Most common sarcoma of retroperitoneum
- Tumor can be as large as 20 cm
- Exhibits wide spectrum of differentiation and phenotypes
- Distinct clinical, radiologic, and cytogenetic features
- Well-differentiated liposarcomas have areas that follow fat attenuation or signal intensity by CT and MRI
- Microscopically: high-grade liposarcoma usually contains pleomorphic adipocytes and lipoblasts
- Well-differentiated liposarcomas may have minimal cytologic atypia of neoplastic adipocytes
- Often require ancillary studies
- Dedifferentiated tumors reveal hypercellularity and significant pleomorphisms
- Indistinguishable from other high-grade sarcomas
- Diagnosis confirmed if amplification of MDM2 and CDK4 genes revealed by in situ hybridization
- Or MDM2 and Cdk4 protein overexpression detected by immunohistochemistry

---

## Primitive Neuroectodermal Tumor (PNET) and Extraosseous Ewing Sarcoma (EES)

- Rare tumors arising from ectopic neural and neuroectodermal tissue
- Can occur anywhere in body
- Grouped together in Ewing sarcoma family
- Similar morphology, immunophenotype, and cytogenetic alterations (t[11;22])
- Aggressive malignancies
- Occur almost exclusively in children and young adults
- Equal sex distribution
- Manifest as large solid masses (mean size 8.2 cm)
- Clinical presentations of pancreatic PNET and EES:
  - Abdominal pain
  - Jaundice
- Grossly: fleshy and lobulated masses
- Frequently invade into peripancreatic soft tissue and adjacent structures
- Microscopically: sheets or nodules of small round blue cells
- Open and coarse chromatin
- Frequent mitoses
- Scant cytoplasm
- Tumor cells show strong and membranous immunoreactivity to CD99
- Cytokeratin may also be positive
- Results should be interpreted with caution in differential diagnosis of undifferentiated and sarcomatous carcinoma
- t(11:22) chromosomal translocation characteristic
- Can be confirmed by in situ hybridization or other genetic testing platforms

---

## Extragastrointestinal Stromal Tumor (E-GIST)

- GISTs: spindle cell neoplasms originating from interstitial cells of Cajal
- Primarily located in GI tract
- Identified in pancreas as well
- E-GISTs represent less than 10% of all GISTs
- Exceedingly rare in pancreas
- E-GISTs of pancreatic origin affect middle-aged adults
- Represent less than 1% of all GISTs
- Primary pancreatic E-GISTs can be large (up to 13 cm)
- Microscopically: tumor cells arranged in fascicles or nests
- Can exhibit spindled or epithelioid morphology with perinuclear vacuoles
- Epithelioid morphology can simulate other primary pancreatic epithelial tumors
- E-GIST cells immunoreactive to CD117, DOG-1, and CD34
- Variable expression of SMA
- Differential diagnosis: leiomyosarcoma (confirmed by immunohistochemistry with expression of muscle markers desmin and SMA)
- Primary desmoid tumor, schwannoma, solitary fibrous tumor, and inflammatory myofibroblast tumor should be considered
- Prognosis of primary pancreatic E-GIST similar to small bowel GIST
  - Relatively aggressive compared with GIST from other sites of GI tract

---

## Solitary Fibrous Tumor (SFT)

- Extrapleural SFT: rare fibroblastic mesenchymal tumor
- Hemangiopericytoma-like branching vascular pattern
- Develops in soft-tissue sites: thorax, extremities, orbit, retroperitoneum
- Pancreatic SFT reported in middle-aged to elderly women (age range 41–78 years)
- Most manifest as slow-growing and painless masses
- Patients with large tumors can present with compressive symptoms
- Rarely hypoglycemia (Doege-Potter syndrome)
- Most SFTs are indolent but should not be considered benign
- May display aggressive local invasion or recur after treatment
- Rare cases of metastases from pancreatic SFTs reported
- Grossly: well circumscribed
- May be exophytic with thin fibrous capsule
- Microscopically: short spindle cells with indistinct cell borders
- Arranged around branching vasculature of variable caliber
- Frequently with staghorn-like appearance
- Aggressive SFTs tend to be hypercellular with increased mitotic count and tumor necrosis
- Immunohistochemical staining: reactivity to CD34, CD99, and STAT6
- EMA and SMA immunoreactive only in small portion of cases
- Differential diagnosis: other primary spindle cell tumors of pancreas

---

## Inflammatory Myofibroblastic Tumor (IMT)

- Low-grade and uncommon mesenchymal neoplasms
- Unknown etiology
- Variable myofibroblastic proliferation and inflammatory infiltrate
- Most commonly occur in mesentery, omentum, retroperitoneum, pelvis, abdominal soft tissues
- In most recent WHO classification of soft tissue tumors:
  - Classified as tumors of intermediate biologic potential
  - Due to tendency for local recurrence and rare metastasis
- Primary pancreatic IMT uncommon
- Slightly more prevalent in women
- Wide age distribution (0.5–70 years)
- Symptoms vague: abdominal pain, weight loss, palpable mass
- When IMT involves pancreatic head, obstructive jaundice may occur
- Prognosis considered favorable after surgical resection
- Rare cases of malignant transformation described

---

## IMT — Pathologic Features

- Grossly: nodular, lobulated masses
- Microscopically: spindled and stellate-shaped cells of variable cellularity
- Myxoid to collagenous stroma
- Background of mixed inflammatory infiltrate
  - Lymphocytes
  - Plasma cells
  - Frequently eosinophils
- Spindle cells can be pleomorphic
- Lymphoid follicles with germinal centers may be present
- Malignant transformation may be associated with:
  - Local invasion
  - Vascular invasion
  - Marked nuclear polymorphism
- Tumor cells immunoreactive with SMA
- About one-third may be positive for cytokeratin
- Many IMTs harbor clonal ALK rearrangements
- Immunoreactivity with anaplastic lymphoma kinase 1 (ALK-1) is diagnostic hallmark
- Differential diagnosis: other primary spindle cell tumors of pancreas
- Undifferentiated and sarcomatous carcinoma of pancreas (much more common primary neoplasm)

---

## Lymphomas

- Most cases of lymphoma found in pancreas associated with systemic disease
- When disease localized to pancreas (even with contiguous nodal involvement or distant spread):
  - Considered primary pancreatic lymphoma (PPL)
- Non-Hodgkin lymphoma most common subtype of PPL
- Histologic subtype: diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL)
- Followed by follicular lymphoma
- PPL accounts for 0.5% of all pancreatic tumors
- Accounts for 0.6% of extranodal lymphomas
- Most PPLs occur in middle-aged patients
- Mean age: 63 years (range 15–85 years)
- More common in immunocompromised patients
  - Associated organ transplantation
  - HIV/AIDS
- Common symptoms: abdominal pain and weight loss
- Jaundice not common despite frequent location in head of pancreas

---

## Lymphomas — Diagnosis and Prognosis

- Treatment and prognosis considerably different from PDAC
- Accurate diagnosis crucial
- PPL has high complete response rate to chemotherapy
- Long disease-specific survival similar to nodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma
- Grossly: soft masses of variable size
- White and fleshy appearance on cut surface
- Higher-grade PPL such as DLBCL can show areas of necrosis
- Pathologically: lymphomas are monoclonal
- Can be characterized by:
  - Histopathology
  - Flow cytometry
  - Immunohistochemistry
  - Cytogenetics
  - Molecular genetic testing
- Infiltrative and sclerosing form of lymphoma can mimic PDAC or pancreatitis
- Distinguishing these entities can be extremely challenging preoperatively
- Given drastic difference in management, biopsy diagnoses may be prudent
  - When radiographic and clinical presentations are not typical for conventional ductal carcinoma

---

## Pseudotumors of the Pancreas — Pseudocyst

- Circumscribed collections of fluid rich in pancreatic enzymes
- With hemorrhage and necrosis
- Usually form as complication of pancreatitis
- In children, frequently occur after abdominal trauma
- Inflamed fibrous capsule with no epithelial lining
- Develop after acute injury resulting in release and activation of pancreatic enzymes
- Leads to tissue necrosis
- Dissolved tissue confined within surrounding granulation tissue
- Ultimately forms encapsulated cyst
- Most patients have clinical history of repeated attacks of AP
- Can be secondary to:
  - Alcohol abuse
  - Duct obstruction by non-neoplastic ideology (e.g., stones)
  - Trauma

---

## Pseudocyst — Pathologic Features

- Macroscopically: most are unilocular
- Varying sizes; some as large as 20 cm
- Cyst contents: hemorrhagic, oily, or necrotic
- Cyst wall: thick and fibrotic
- Microscopically: cyst wall lacks any epithelial lining
- Composed of organized granulation tissue
- Varying degrees of inflammatory infiltrate and fibroblastic proliferation
- Aggregates of foamy histiocytes and fat necrosis can be observed in inner cyst wall
- Differential diagnosis: neoplastic cystic lesions of pancreas
  - Mucinous cystic neoplasm
  - Solid pseudopapillary tumor
  - Serous cystadenoma
- Radiographic diagnosis can be challenging
- Established clinical history of repetitive episodes of AP or trauma can facilitate diagnosis
- Cyst fluid aspirations accompanying cytology specimen can be used for:
  - Measurement of amylase and CEA levels
  - Other molecular tests
- Markedly elevated amylase along with clinical history could bolster diagnosis of pseudocysts
- Elevated CEA levels and other molecular profiles suggest potential mucinous neoplasms

---

## Retention Cyst

- Usually unilocular
- Developed by dilatation of obstructed pancreatic main or branch duct
- Due to stones, inflammation, or tumors
- Although isolated retention cysts are benign
- Can be observed distal to pancreatic adenocarcinoma (impedes duct proximally)
- Multiple retention cysts with viscose content can be seen in patients with cystic fibrosis
- Thin walled
- Vary in size from incidental microscopic findings (a few millimeters) to grossly detectable cysts
- Careful examination of pancreatic duct proximal to cyst is prudent
  - To exclude potential occult adenocarcinoma
- Inner cyst wall has smooth and shiny appearance
- Cyst lined by a single layer of cuboidal epithelium mirroring normal PD epithelium
- Epithelium can exhibit low-grade PanIN
- Raises differential diagnosis of true neoplastic lesions such as MCN and branch-duct IPMN
- MCNs usually occur in women and have characteristic cellular ovarian-like stroma
- Distinguishing between retention cyst with PanIN and branch-duct IPMN can be challenging
- Latter usually has at least focal papillae formation
- May be associated with multiple, microscopically dilated ducts in vicinity

---

## Figure 59.16 — Pancreatic Retention Cyst

- Gross photo of a retention cyst formed secondary to obstruction by stones

---

## Chronic Pancreatitis

- Benign chronic inflammatory and fibrosing conditions of pancreas
- May be difficult to distinguish from carcinomas
- Both clinically and pathologically
- CP associated with alcohol abuse, ductal obstruction, or other inflammatory conditions
- May lead to localized fibrosis and mass-forming lesions
- Certain subtypes of CP especially inclined to form pseudotumors
- Simulate malignant carcinomas

---

## Groove Pancreatitis (GP)

- Localized form of CP
- Occurs in pancreaticoduodenal space
- Between medial wall of first and second portions of duodenum
- And superior-posterior aspect of head of pancreas
- Also known as:
  - Paraduodenal pancreatitis
  - Cystic dystrophy of heterotopic pancreas
  - Myoadenomatosis
  - Periampullary duodenal wall cyst
  - Pancreatic hamartoma of duodenum
- Etiology multifactorial
- Involves structural and anatomic factors
- Stasis of pancreatic secretions
- Leads to PD obstruction with extravasation of activated proteolytic enzymes
- Triggers pancreatitis and cascade of chronic inflammation, cyst formation, and fibrosis
- Primary or secondary obstruction of accessory duct of Santorini and its outlet minor papilla appears to be leading cause
- Supported by frequent finding of cystic dilatation of accessory duct on pathologic examination
- Heterotopic pancreatic tissue and Brunner's gland hyperplasia that infiltrate wall of second portion of duodenum can lead to partial obstruction of minor papilla
- Minor papilla lacks well-developed sphincter
  - More susceptible to partial obstruction

---

## GP — Clinical Features

- Patients typically males in fifth or sixth decade
- Most have history of chronic alcohol and/or nicotine abuse
- Up to 50% may have history of prior episodes of AP
- Clinical presentation may mimic AP
  - Severe abdominal pain
  - Nausea
  - Vomiting
- Often has more chronic and relapsing course
