- Repeated episodes of abdominal pain and weight loss
- Jaundice may be present with involvement of CBD and postinflammatory strictures
- Symptoms can simulate those of PDAC
- Variability of GP on imaging analysis can render definitive preoperative diagnosis challenging
- Particularly with differential diagnosis of pancreatic or ampullary carcinomas

---

## GP — Pathologic Features

- Macroscopic findings:
  - Thickening of medial aspect of duodenal wall
  - Mucosal nodularity in vicinity of minor papilla
  - Ampulla of Vater usually unremarkable
  - Fibrotic mass in pancreaticoduodenal space
  - Some degree of microcystic change
  - Foci of pancreatic parenchyma can be found within fibrotic mass
- Microscopically (pseudotumor of GP):
  - Varying amounts of dense fibrosis
  - Lymphoplasmacytic or histiocytic type inflammation
  - Granulation tissue
  - Microabscesses
  - Brunner's gland hyperplasia
  - Smooth muscle hyperplasia
  - Myoadenomatosis of duodenal wall
- Fibrosis may lead to duodenal encasement and stenosis
  - Resultant gastric outlet obstruction
- Biliary obstruction may occur when lesion extends to CBD

---

## Autoimmune Pancreatitis (AIP)

- Also known as lymphoplasmacytic sclerosing pancreatitis (LPSP)
- Or nonalcoholic destructive pancreatitis
- Chronic inflammatory condition
- Increasingly recognized as uncommon but important cause of recurrent AP or painless jaundice
- Can be radiographically and endoscopically mistaken for PDAC
- Reported to account for up to 2% of all cases of CP
- Etiology considered autoimmune
- Demonstrated by presence of lymphoplasmacytic infiltration on histology

**Two clinical subtypes:**
- **Type 1:** IgG4-related pancreatitis
  - Associated with high serum IgG4 concentration
  - IgG4-bearing plasma cell infiltration of pancreas
  - Background of lymphoplasmacytic sclerosing pancreatitis
- **Type 2:** Idiopathic duct-centric pancreatitis
  - Granulocytic epithelial lesions in pancreatic duct
  - Without IgG4-positive cells or systemic involvement

---

## AIP — Clinical Features and Diagnosis

- Patients can present with recurrent episodes of abdominal pain
- With or without attacks of pancreatitis
- Obstructive jaundice common presentation
- Can be accompanied by nonspecific symptoms:
  - Nausea
  - Vomiting
  - Loss of appetite
  - Weight loss
- Responds generally well to treatment with corticosteroids
- Favorable prognosis
- Diagnostic criteria include:
  - Imaging of pancreas and pancreatic duct
  - Serologic studies of IgG4 levels
  - Histopathology
  - Presence of other associated conditions
    - Multifocal fibrosclerosis syndrome
    - Retroperitoneal and mediastinal fibrosis
    - Riedel thyroiditis
    - Inflammatory pseudotumor of orbit
    - Sclerosing cholangitis

---

## AIP — Pathologic Features

- If resected, pancreatic parenchyma may or may not have discrete lesions
- Usually have a rigid appearance
- Microscopically:
  - Dense periductal and perivenular lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates
  - Obliterative phlebitis
  - Presence of both interlobular and intralobular fibrosis
  - Acinar atrophy
- Immunohistochemistry for IgG4 reveals numerous positive plasma cells
- Diffusely distributed in periductal infiltrates in Type 1 AIP

---

## Figure 59.17 — LPSP Macroscopic Appearance

- Gross photo of a pancreatoduodenectomy with rigid pancreatic parenchyma without discrete lesion/mass
- Both pancreatic duct and common bile duct are not obstructed

---

## Figure 59.18 — LPSP Histopathology

- **A:** Dense periductal lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate
- **B:** Dense perivenular lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate (venulitis)
- **C:** Interstitial and periductal fibrosis
- **D:** Diffuse and intense staining for IgG4 by immunohistochemistry

---

## Heterotopic Spleen

- Nodules of heterotopic spleen tissue (splenules) can be present within pancreatic parenchyma
- Most located in distal pancreas
- Radiographically: splenules may appear as solid primary pancreatic neoplasm
- Macroscopically: well-circumscribed, red-tan soft lesions
- Usually less than 3 cm in diameter
- Microscopically: made up of unremarkable spleen tissue

---

## Hamartoma

- Benign tumor-like nodules
- Composed of overgrowth of mature parenchymal elements
- Usually acini and/or ducts with distorted architecture
- Lacking discrete islets of Langerhans
- Macroscopically: sharply demarcated nodules
- Average diameter: 3.3 cm
- Cut surface may be solid or focally cystic
- Microscopically: epithelial elements and fibrous stroma
- Epithelial elements (acini or ducts) tend to distribute in periphery of tumor
- Fibrotic stroma situated more centrally

---

## Metastatic Tumors — Overview

- Most common metastatic tumors involving pancreas:
  - Carcinomas of lung
  - Carcinomas of GI origin
  - Lymphomas
  - Renal cell carcinoma
- Secondary tumors account for almost half of pancreatic masses detected at autopsy
- Common metastatic tumors in surgical resection specimens:
  - Lymphomas
  - Renal cell carcinomas
  - Melanomas
- Resected either as result of:
  - Occult primary tumors
  - Unrecognized clinical history of primary tumors
  - Therapeutic modality
  - Complications caused by secondary tumors
  - Curative attempts
- In these situations, tumors usually solitary with no other detectable masses
- Lymphomas and renal cell carcinomas particularly prone to involve pancreas in absence of other metastatic foci
  - Mimicking primary carcinoma of pancreas

---

## Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma

- Often involve pancreas as solitary mass
- In absence of other metastatic foci
- Amenable to surgical resection
- Associated with long-term survival
- Clear cell carcinoma most common subtype to metastasize to pancreas
- Can manifest more than a decade after initial presentation and diagnosis of primary kidney tumor
- Macroscopically: well-circumscribed, fleshy, bright yellow-tan lesions
- Microscopically: tumor cells arranged in nests, sheets, or cords
- Rich sinusoid-pattern of vascular network
- Prominent clear cytoplasm
- Differential diagnosis:
  - Primary pancreatic well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor of clear cell subtype
  - Other solid tumors with clear cytoplasm
    - Ductal adenocarcinoma with clear cell appearance
    - Solid serous adenoma
    - Clear cell variant of solid pseudopapillary tumor
    - PEComa

---

## Metastatic Melanoma

- Metastatic melanoma in pancreas of unknown primary site is rare
- Major primary sites of melanoma metastasizing to pancreas: cutaneous and ocular
- In up to 13% of cases, primary site may not be identified
  - Suggests possibility of misdiagnosis of primary pancreatic malignancy
- Some propose patients with isolated pancreatic melanoma may benefit from surgery
  - When complete resection is possible
- Patients with unknown primary melanoma appear to have equivalent or better outcomes
  - Than patients with known primaries of similar stage
- Gross appearance may be black if tumor is intensely pigmented
- Microscopic examination: wide spectrum of morphologic features
- Tumor cells generally not arranged in particular pattern
- Display diffuse and noncohesive infiltration
- Malignant melanocytes described as having large round nuclei with macronucleoli
- Can notoriously mimic many types of malignancies
  - Carcinoma
  - Sarcoma
  - Lymphoma
  - Particularly when tumor is not pigmented
- Immunoreactivity for melanocytic markers (S100, SOX10, Melan-A, HMB45)
- Negative labeling for cytokeratin can confirm diagnosis

---

## Tumors of Ampulla and Periampulla — Introduction

- Variety of neoplasms can arise at:
  - Ampulla of Vater
  - Minor papillae
  - Surrounding periampullary duodenum
  - At confluence of pancreatic and biliary ducts
- Ampulla comprised of several types of epithelia:
  - Intestinal-type duodenal mucosa covering papilla
  - PD epithelium
  - Biliary epithelium of distal CBD
  - Epithelium lining common channel uniting PD and CBD within duodenal wall
- Lining epithelia of PD, CBD, and common channel are histologically similar
  - Pancreatobiliary-type epithelium
- Neoplasms arising in ampulla may have predominantly:
  - Intestinal phenotype
  - Pancreatobiliary phenotype
  - Mixed phenotype
- Most ampullary neoplasms are adenocarcinomas or precursor lesions
- Rare specific types of neuroendocrine tumors also involve this region
- Tumors often extend to involve ampulla, pancreas, distal bile duct, and duodenum

---

## Ampullary Adenoma and Noninvasive Intraampullary Papillary-Tubular Neoplasm

**Two subtypes based on location and histologic phenotype:**

1. **Intestinal-type adenomas**
   - Arising from duodenal surface mucosa overlying ampulla
   - Similar to colorectal adenomas
   - Can occur in association with FAP or Lynch syndromes

2. **Intraampullary papillary-tubular neoplasm (IAPN)**
   - Arising within intraampullary channel (distal CBD and PD)
   - Usually pancreatobiliary-type

- Most patients with ampullary adenomas and IAPNs are asymptomatic when tumors are small
- Larger tumors can cause:
  - Jaundice
  - Cholangitis
  - Pancreatitis
  - Secondary to obstruction of CBD or PD

---

## Ampullary Adenoma and IAPN — Microscopic Features

**Intestinal-type ampullary adenomas:**
- Resemble colorectal counterparts
- May have tubular, villous, or tubulovillous configuration
- Intestinal-type epithelium reveals nuclear pseudostratification of tall-columnar cells with elongated nuclei
- Degree of dysplasia assessed based on cytologic atypia and architectural complexity
- High-grade dysplasia: complex, cribriform glands with significant nuclear atypia and loss of epithelial polarity
- Immunohistochemistry: expression of intestinal markers (CK20, MUC2, CDX2)
- Generally lack expression of CK7 and MUC1

**IAPNs:**
- Defined as predominantly pancreatobiliary type
- Nearly half of cases have mixed pancreatobiliary and intestinal phenotype
- Form exophytic polypoid masses in ampulla
- Grow within ampullary channel with minimal or no involvement of PD, CBD, or duodenal papilla
- Leads to protuberant ampulla with widened orifice seen by endoscopy
- Microscopically: markedly complex villous and papillary architecture
- Branching papillae lined by cuboidal cells
- Round and atypical nuclei lacking nuclear pseudostratification of intestinal-type adenomas
- Most IAPNs (> 80%) have both low-grade and high-grade dysplasia
- Degree of dysplasia assessed by architecture complexity and nuclear atypia

---

## Figure 59.19 — Ampullary Adenoma

- **A:** An adenoma arising from duodenal surface mucosa overlying ampulla at convergence of distal common bile duct (CBD) and pancreatic duct (PD)
- **B:** An intraampullary papillary-tubular neoplasm arising within intraampullary channel (distal CBD and PD)

---

## Ampullary Adenoma and IAPN — Treatment and Prognosis

- May be treated effectively by endoscopic resection or transduodenal papillectomy
- Rather than pancreatoduodenectomy
- Specimens from these procedures should be carefully examined to determine:
  - Complete excision of lesion
  - Search for occult foci of carcinoma
- Patients with noninvasive carcinomas have very good prognosis
- May occasionally develop recurrence in long-term follow-up
- Presence of carcinoma can give rise to recurrence after local therapy
- More radical operative approach commonly preferred

---

## Ampullary Adenocarcinoma — Epidemiology and Clinical Features

- Ampulla is most common site for small intestinal adenocarcinoma
- Accounts for 15% of all pancreatoduodenectomies performed
- Because of complex anatomy at papilla and biliary/pancreatic effluents:
  - Many carcinomas arising in duodenum, pancreas, or CBD can secondarily extend into ampulla
  - May be incorrectly designated as ampullary primary tumor
- Establishment of tumor's ampullary origin may be challenging preoperatively
- May ultimately require examination of pancreatoduodenectomy specimen
- Median age for ampullary adenocarcinoma: approximately mid-60s
- Typical presentation: biliary obstruction and associated symptoms
  - Cholestasis
  - Jaundice
  - Lead to relatively early diagnosis
- Periampullary duodenal subtype carcinomas can cause GI bleeding
  - Because of mucosal ulceration

---

## Ampullary Adenocarcinoma — Prognosis

- Patients with ampullary carcinomas have relatively favorable survival prognosis
- Compared with those with pancreatic ductal carcinomas
- 5-year survival rate: 50% with localized disease
- 5-year survival rate: 28% with lymph node metastases

**Ampullary adenocarcinoma can arise from:**
1. Periampullary duodenal mucosa
   - Usually with associated adenoma
   - Prevalent in patients with FAP
2. Intraampullary channel
   - Either with associated IAPN
   - Or flat dysplasia of ampullary ducts

---

## Ampullary Adenocarcinoma — Pathologic Features

- Macroscopic appearance depends on specific subtype
- When tumor involves surface duodenal mucosa:
  - Can form polypoid or ulcerated mass evident at endoscopic evaluation
- Intraampullary carcinomas:
  - Relatively small
  - Covered by intact duodenal mucosa
  - May only present as subtle and raised nodule elevated from duodenal mucosa
- Microscopically: most have gland formation
- Either intestinal or pancreatobiliary phenotype
- About 30% to 40% of cases have mixed phenotype

---

## Figure 59.20 — Ampullary Adenocarcinoma in a Whipple Specimen

- **A:** An adenocarcinoma protruding from the ampulla
- **B:** Bi-valved pancreatectomy specimen showing the tumor at the ampulla and distal CBD and pancreatic duct, causing proximal ductal dilatation

---

## Ampullary Adenocarcinoma — Intestinal Type

- Usually arises in association with an ampullary adenoma
- Resembles large intestinal adenocarcinoma counterpart
- Tumors composed of cribriform glands with tall columnar cells
- Elongated nuclei
- Intestinal phenotype confirmed by immunohistochemistry
- Positive reactivity for CDX2 and MUC2

---

## Ampullary Adenocarcinoma — Pancreatobiliary Type

- Shares morphologic features and immunophenotype with PDAC
- Tumors composed of simple or branching glands
- Lined by a single layer of cuboidal cells
- Round or pleomorphic nuclei
- Prominent stromal desmoplasia
- Tumor cells immunoreactive to CK7 and MUC1

---

## Ampullary Neuroendocrine Carcinoma

- Poorly differentiated NECs represent rare phenotype of ampullary carcinoma
- Many NECs arise in association with an adenoma
- May have mixed components of glandular or squamous differentiation
- **Small-cell carcinoma subtype:**
  - Fusiform cells with minimal cytoplasm
  - Hyperchromatic chromatin
  - Nuclear molding
- **Large-cell variant NECs:**
  - Moderate amounts of cytoplasm
  - Round nuclei with prominent nucleoli
- Poorly differentiated NECs are high-grade, aggressive malignancies
- Geographic necrosis commonly observed
- Neuroendocrine differentiation required for diagnosis
- Generally assessed by checking expression of chromogranin or synaptophysin

---

## Other Histology Variants of Ampullary Carcinoma

- Many other less common histologic variants described:
  - Adenosquamous carcinoma
  - Mucinous adenocarcinoma
  - Signet ring cell carcinoma
  - Medullary carcinoma
  - Undifferentiated carcinoma
- Although morphologic features of each subtype are distinctive
- They do not have specific clinical or genetic differences
- Compared with more common histologic subtypes

---

## Ampullary Neuroendocrine Tumors — Epidemiology and Clinical Features

- Duodenal NETs are rare among intestinal NETs (2%–3%)
- Represent most diverse group of neoplasms
- Often present with unusual clinical features and unique pathologic characteristics
- Involve several subtypes of neuroendocrine cells
- Associated with multiple hereditary associations
- Ampullary NETs predominantly involve submucosa and muscularis of duodenum and ampulla
- Extension into mucosa with subsequent bleeding can occur
- Diagnosis can be established via endoscopic mucosal biopsy
- Ampullary duodenum is primary location of:
  - Somatostatin-producing D-cell NET (somatostatinoma)
  - Gangliocytoparaganglioma
  - Constitute about 30% of all duodenal NETs
- Both entities have known associations with hereditary conditions of NF1 and MEN1
- Hereditary association much less common in gangliocytoparaganglioma

---

## Ampullary Somatostatinoma vs. Pancreatic Somatostatinoma

- **Pancreatic counterpart:**
  - Extremely rare
  - Presents with somatostatin hypersecretion-related symptoms
    - Diarrhea
    - Cholelithiasis
    - Dyspepsia
    - Diabetes
- **Duodenal somatostatinoma:**
  - Almost never functional
  - Given exclusive location at or around major or minor ampulla
  - Frequently cause obstructive symptoms
    - AP
    - Jaundice
    - Intestinal bleeding

---

## Ampullary NET — Pathologic Features

- Somatostatin-producing D-cell NETs commonly exhibit glandular growth pattern
- Psammomatous calcifications present in lumen of glands
- Also known as glandular carcinoid and psammomatous somatostatinoma
- Usually less than 1 to 3 cm in size
- Typically located in either major or minor ampulla or periampullary region
- Presence of calcification phenomena associated with:
  - 100% of NF1-associated tumors
  - 60% of sporadic somatostatinomas
- When present in submucosa, may have appearance mimicking benign Brunner's glands of duodenum
- Tumor does not form well-circumscribed border
- Infiltrates deeply into smooth muscle of Sphincter of Oddi
- Abutting or invading pancreas common without eliciting desmoplastic reaction
- Negative deep resection margins can be difficult to achieve from local excisions
  - Either endoscopic intervention or papillectomy
- Given combined clinical presentation of jaundice and glandular-forming histology
  - Not uncommon for somatostatinomas to be misinterpreted as adenocarcinoma of ampulla in biopsy specimens
- Cytologic level: relatively homogenous and round to ovoid nuclei
- Stippled chromatin
- Moderate amount of granular cytoplasm
- Tumor necrosis almost never seen in small tumors
- Mitotic activity in range of 0 to 2 mitoses/10 high power fields (WHO G1 grade)
- Ki67 proliferative index > 2% may place them in WHO G2 grade

## Gangliocytoparaganglioma (GCP)

- May present as polypoid or pedunculated ampullary or periampullary lesion
- Usually measure 1 to 3 cm
- Unique type of neuroendocrine tumor with trilineage differentiation:
  - Neuroendocrine epithelium
  - Schwannian/nerve sheath
  - Ganglion components
- Immunohistochemically:
  - Tumor cells generally reactive for chromogranin and synaptophysin
  - Epithelial component may not be immunoreactive to cytokeratin in up to 50% of cases
  - Tumor cells usually positive for pancreatic polypeptide, somatostatin, or VIP
  - Schwannian component immunoreactive for S100

---

## Figure 59.22 — Ampullary Gangliocytoparaganglioma (GCP)

- **A:** Endoscopic appearance of a polypoid mass
- **B:** GCP with trilineage differentiation including neuroendocrine epithelium (upper left), spindled schwannian/nerve sheath, and ganglion components (lower right)

## Ampullary NET — Prognosis

- Lymph node metastasis occurs in approximately 30%
- Liver metastasis occurs in approximately 5%
- Most patients have favorable outcomes after complete removal of disease
- May require pancreatoduodenectomy because of ampullary location of tumor
- 10-year survival: over 70%

---

## Summary — Key Points (1)

- PanIN is the precursor lesion of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
- High-grade PanIN (PanIN-3) is carcinoma in situ
- PDAC is the most common pancreatic neoplasm (> 90%)
- Most PDAC harbor KRAS mutations (> 90%)
- Tumor suppressor genes: TP53, SMAD4, CDKN2A
- Colloid carcinoma has better prognosis than conventional PDAC
- IPMN, IOPN, and ITPN are intraductal neoplasms with cystic features
- GNAS mutation is unique to IPMN
- MCN occurs almost exclusively in women; ovarian-like stroma is defining
- Serous cystadenoma is benign; VHL-associated cases are multifocal

---

## Summary — Key Points (2)

- Pancreatic NETs are classified as well-differentiated PanNET or poorly differentiated PanNEC
- PanNETs: MEN1, DAXX, ATRX mutations; not KRAS/TP53/SMAD4
- Acinar cell carcinoma: trypsin/chymotrypsin positive; BCL10 positive
- Pancreatoblastoma: squamoid nests; children; AFP elevated
- SPN: young women; β-catenin nuclear; chromogranin negative
- Mesenchymal tumors of pancreas are rare (1%–2%)
- Lymphomas: DLBCL most common; PPL is 0.5% of pancreatic tumors
- Pseudocysts lack epithelial lining; retention cysts have cuboidal epithelium
- AIP: Type 1 (IgG4-related) and Type 2 (duct-centric)
- Metastatic tumors to pancreas: lung, GI, lymphoma, RCC, melanoma

---

## Summary — Key Points (3)

- Ampullary adenomas: intestinal type and IAPN (pancreatobiliary type)
- Ampullary adenocarcinoma: intestinal or pancreatobiliary phenotype
- Ampullary NETs: somatostatinoma and gangliocytoparaganglioma
- Somatostatinomas: glandular pattern, psammomatous calcifications, NF1 association
- GCP: trilineage differentiation (neuroendocrine, schwannian, ganglion)
- Prognosis of ampullary carcinomas is better than PDAC
- Accurate diagnosis is crucial for appropriate management
- Molecular testing increasingly important for targeted therapy
